newsitem.title: POLAND: Foreign investment in Poland exceeds $10 billion. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Poland exceeds $10 billion. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]

text.p: Foreign investment in Poland has exceeded $10 billion since 1990 and is set to gain pace as investors are lured by the country's regained financial credibility and stability, a government agency said on Friday.
"Foreign investment broke the magical barrier of $10 billion in July...and will grow further," Waldemar Dabrowski, president of the Polish Foreign Investment Agency (PAIZ), told a news conference.

He said investors -- who in the early 1990s favoured Hungary and the Czech Republic, two other Eastern European economic leaders -- are now turning to Poland, the biggest market in the region except for the former Soviet countries.

Since the fall of communism in 1989, foreign direct investors have brought nearly $11 billion to Hungary and more than $5 billion to the Czech Republic, which means Poland still badly trails the two countries in per capita investment inflow.

But Dabrowski said Poland would significantly improve its ranking over the next few years, especially after it opens its banking and insurance sectors to foreign capital in 1999 under agreements with the European Union.

This year alone foreign investment should reach $4 billion, fuelled by sales of two tobacco plants to United States' Philip Morris and German's Reemtsma for $227 million and $130 million respectively, and by privatisations in the cement sector.
"They (investors) see that order is being introduced into the economy, politics are more stable, macroeconomic discipline is being maintained... and inflation is falling" he said.
Poland's inflation was curbed to 21.6 percent (corrects from 20.6 percent) in December last year and 19.5 percent in June from 29.5 in December 1994.
The budget deficit has stayed below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), as recommended by the EU's Maastricht treaty, for the last two years.

But Dabrowski said the main reason why foreign investment jumped to $10.2 billion from $4.3 billion in December 1994, was Poland's settling accounts with foreign government and banking creditors and returning to international financial markets.

Poland's signing of a debt-rescheduling deal with foreign banks in 1994 paved the way for last year's successful $250 million eurobond issue. "Our economy is increasingly being treated as reliable," Dabrowski said.
He said that while in the early 1990s foreign investment came mostly from small companies, it was now dominated by large corporations, notably those from the United States.

U.S. firms led foreign investors, with direct investment of $2.4 billion and commitments of $2.9 billion since 1990, followed by multi-national corporations, with $1.5 billion and $164 billion respectively.

The biggest single investor is Italy's Fiat Spa, which has pumped in $702 million and pledged to bring $1.1 billion more, followed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), with $608 million.
Dutch ING Groep, owner of Bank Slaski SA, ranked third with an investment of $343 million.
